newsitem.title: UK: Rocky road, little time for NATO and Russia.
newsitem.headline: Rocky road, little time for NATO and Russia.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

The new year has got off to a bad start for NATO and Russia, with Moscow pushing hard for more concessions over the alliance's planned enlargement and Western allies worried about how to deal with their former Cold War foe.

After months of confusing and sometimes contradictory signals, Russia appears to have laid down a hard line as the two sides prepare to negotiate on how their relationship -- the key to European security -- should work.

President Boris Yeltsin, now back in the saddle after heart surgery, told German Chancellor Helmut Kohl at weekend talks that Russia wanted what amounts to the right of joint decisions with NATO on important security issues.

Moscow wanted a legally-binding mechanism to make sure this would happen, as well as assurances that there would be no expansion of NATO's military into new members from Eastern Europe, the sources told Reuters on Monday.
Russia's continued opposition to enlargement, which Moscow says represents a threat to its security, was underlined on Monday at a meeting between Yeltsin and his top advisers.
Since the 16-nation alliance first announced two years ago that it was prepared to take in new members, Russia has won some concessions from NATO through its strident opposition.

Some Western diplomats believe this has encouraged Yeltsin and his top officials to push for even more, while others say the Russian leader has no choice given that he is under pressure from a suspicious military and defence ministry establishment.
Either way, NATO has to tread a very thin line -- and it has to solve the problem fast.
Invitations to potential new members will be handed out at a NATO summit that has been scheduled for July in Madrid.
The allies have agreed that they must have the details of their new relationship with Russia worked out by then, so that it can be presented as part of an even-handed approach.
The alliance has solemnly promised that new members will join. Diplomats say Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic will probably all be members by 1999. But what will be the price?
"The question is whether the Russians will now be able to get anything else out of us, given that we have committed ourselves to a timetable in the runup to the summit," said one diplomat.
"It's hard to see why Kohl seemed so confident of sucess after the talks with Yeltsin."

Giving the Russians too much say in important NATO decisions will lay the alliance open to charges of weakness, particularly from Eastern European countries which hope to join in the future and which remember -- with no hint of fondness -- the days when Moscow ruled them more or less directly.

Diplomats say many smaller NATO allies are also worried that a "directorate" of big powers could emerge, with the United States, Germany, France, Britain and Russia taking major decisions about issues that affect the alliance.
However, telling the Russians to mind their own business and ignoring their concerns while going ahead with enlargement is widely seen as a dangerous game within NATO.
Russia would be able to do little in practical terms beyond hampering efforts at arms control and perhaps encouraging other former Soviet republics to forge closer military ties.
NATO allies still want to build real cooperation with Russia and avoid any risk of renewed confrontation.
Kohl and other Western leaders believe there is now a unique chance to make Russia part of a new, secure Europe and they will be pushing hard to change attitudes in Moscow.
French President Jacques Chirac and British Prime Minister John Major are expected to meet Yeltsin in the coming weeks, while a U.S.-Russian summit is expected in March.

While NATO allies are virtually certain to oppose the latest Russian demands, diplomats say they will have to strike the right balance soon -- even though they do not yet agree among themselves about where that balance should be.
Diplomats say Yeltsin's approach in his talks with Kohl appeared designed to put maximum pressure on the allies before they have managed to agree among themselves.

NATO has already agreed that it will offer Russia a special relationship, probably in the form of a charter that will allow regular consultations without legal commitments. Two years ago, the alliance was not even willing to offer that much.
But it is not yet clear how it will work and how much real influence Russia will have. REUTER
